new.n: Keel Ridge Mine: the 1883 cave-in tomb of eight miners
new.pl: About two blocks north of US-2/141, half a mile east of the Iron Mountain city limits
new.v: A miners' grave: look only
new.st: The Keel Ridge Mine opened in 1880 and had shipped 53,445 tons of iron ore by spring 1883. With the ore worked out and the ground sinking, the pumps were pulled, and on 10 April 1883 the surface caved in and swallowed eight miners about 200 ft down. Their bodies were never recovered and now lie under about 100 ft of water. The old rail bed, stone foundations, ore piles, a shaft opening and deep cave holes remain.
new.t: LOOK ONLY. It is the grave of eight men, and the cave pits are unstable and deep. Do not hunt here.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots
acc: Miners' grave and unstable cave pits: look only, never dig or detect

new.n: Sturgeon Mills and the lost camp payroll
new.pl: Between Norway and Vulcan on the Chicago & North Western, by John O'Callaghan's 1878 sawmill

new.st: Sturgeon was split in half by the Chicago & North Western, with a spur to the lumber mill; the company houses were later moved to Vulcan, and the last resident left with the last house. Old-timers told of a lost payroll of more than $100,000 from one of the camps. Some say it was found, others that it never was.

new.n: Huron Bay & Iron Range Railway: the summit cut and its construction camp (1890-93)
new.pl: Near Mount Arvon, at the 1,960-ft divide at the head of the Slate River
new.v: Construction-camp losses: tools, spikes, bottles, coins and blacksmith scrap
new.st: The "ghost railroad": a $2,000,000, 35-mile line from Champion to an ore dock at Huron Bay that never ran a revenue train, and its one test run went into the ditch (Dodge, reprinting the L'Anse Sentinel of 23 September 1964). Near the summit cut, blasted through 40,000 cubic yards of granite, are signs of a big camp with a blacksmith shop and log buildings, and workers' huts built partly underground. A 500-ft rock fill and half a mile of decayed cedar trestle piling remain along the grade.
new.t: Trace the grade on an old topo or air photo and look for the big rock cut; the hut pits and the blacksmith flat beside it are the ground. Mostly forest land: check who owns it first.

fr-skanee-1871-lumber-camp-on-huron-bay.st: Dodge (1973): Skanee was named for the Skåne district of Sweden; a handful of residents and a hundred or more visitors celebrated Arvon Township's first 100 years here in July 1971. Old-timers told the story of lumberjack John "Silver Jack" Driscoll, who came back to camp from a stream in the Huron Mountains with a pocketful of silver nuggets and never told where. He died at the Ballenger Hotel in L'Anse on 1 April 1895, after the Yellow Dog River drive, and lies in an unmarked spot in the Old L'Anse Cemetery. Skanee people also told "O'Neil gold" legends, and gold, silver and (in 1941) uranium have all been found in the Huron Mountains.
fr-skanee-1871-lumber-camp-on-huron-bay.t: The nugget and gold stories are legends from one source; the Old L'Anse Cemetery is look-only.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

vs-2129316.st: Dodge (1973): Aura was settled in 1914 on the Duluth, South Shore & Atlantic and M-41 in L'Anse Township, 12 miles northwest of L'Anse. By 1927 it had about 200 people, a daily bus to L'Anse, Catholic, Lutheran and Methodist churches and the New Mazda movie theater; in 1973 only Dan's General Store, with the post office, was still open, across from the empty Aura Co-op Store.

vs-2129275.st: Dodge (1973): Zeba, "little river", was an Indian mission with 300 or more people. Father Baraga had a mission here briefly in 1831 before moving across the bay to Assinins, and in 1832 the first Indian church on Lake Superior, a Methodist mission, was built here; it was rebuilt in 1835 and 1848, and the small yellow church standing on the same site dates from 1888.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots
vs-2129275.t: The mission ground and churchyard are look-only.

vs-2128842.st: Dodge (1973): Loretto, between Waucedah and Vulcan on US-2, was named for the Loretto mine and was served by two railroads, the Wisconsin & Michigan (the "Wisky-Mich") and the Chicago & North Western. It kept about 500 people as late as 1940; the Wisky-Mich tracks were pulled up in 1971, and a few original buildings and families remained in 1973.

vs-2126082.st: Dodge (1973): Dunham was on the Chicago & North Western in Bessemer Township, 17 miles southeast of Bessemer; its post office opened on 6 October 1902. In 1905 it had about 200 people, with the Ashland Iron & Steel Company's store, a blacksmith and a school.

vs-2126079.st: Dodge (1973): Gogebic Station was established in Ontonagon County before Gogebic County was formed; its post office opened on 4 June 1886, with Frank Crowe as postmaster, and the name was changed to Gogebic on 25 May 1894.

vs-2126069.st: Dodge (1973): Thomaston, on the Soo Line in Wakefield Township 8 miles from Bessemer, was settled about 1890 and got its post office on 7 November 1891. In 1893 it had about 150 people, with two restaurants and L. W. Dodendorf as postmaster and railroad agent.

vs-1926616.st: Dodge (1973): Tula got its post office on 5 February 1907. In 1915 it had about 100 people, on the Soo Line 9 miles from Wakefield, around the Tula Lumber Company; the post office closed on 16 December 1916 and Tula became a rural route of Thomaston.

vs-2124167.st: Dodge (1973): Askel, in Portage Township 20 miles south of Houghton, was settled in 1890. In 1915 it had a blacksmith, a flour mill, a threshing and milling company and a co-op store; by 1927 it was down to about 25 people, with tri-weekly mail on the Soo Line.

cmine-19.st: Dodge (1973): Atlantic Mine was settled in 1865, a mining village of about 600 in Adams Township on the Copper Range Railroad, 3 miles south of Houghton. cmine-20.st: Dodge (1973): Baltic had about 1,200 people in 1905, on the Copper Range Railroad in Adams Township, 6 miles southwest of Houghton, around the Baltic Mining Company. By 1918 it had grown to about 3,000.

m-ghost-donken.st: Dodge (1973): Donken (also spelled Donkyn and Donkeyn) had about 100 people in 1927, on the Copper Range Railroad in Elm River Township, 20 miles south of Houghton, with the Case Lumber Company's mill and store, a hotel and a barber. Its post office ran from 1920 to about 1935, and in 1968 five postal boxes were still in use.

cmine-15.st: Dodge (1973): Franklin Mine, formerly the Arcadian Mine, had about 500 people in 1910, on the Mineral Range Railroad in Franklin Township, 2 miles north of Hancock, and was linked to Houghton by an electric railway. It had the Franklin Mining Company, a saloon, a barber, a physician and a general store, and later the Houghton County detention hospital.

vs-2124160.st: Dodge (1973): Freda had about 500 people in 1910, on the Copper Range Railroad in Stanton Township, 17 miles west of Houghton, with a Congregational church and the Champion Copper Company's stamp mill (and its Lake Shore band); by 1917 it also had a Catholic church, hotels and a movie theater. cd-centennial-mill-point-mills.st: Dodge (1973): In 1905 Point Mills had about 300 people in Torch Lake Township, 7 miles from Houghton and 3 from Dollar Bay, around the Arcadian and Franklin stamp mills, with a boarding house, saloon, livery, general store and school.

vs-2129425.st: Dodge (1973): Basswood was a stop on the Chicago & North Western between Beechwood and Elmwood, with no post office. In the logging days a few lumberjacks built rough shacks here, and Archie McKrause homesteaded the land; nothing remained by 1973.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

vs-2129433.st: Dodge (1973): Pentoga had about 250 people in 1905, on the Chicago & North Western in Stambaugh Township, 15 miles southwest of Crystal Falls, with the Brule River House and Pentoga Hotel, a sawmill, general stores, a livery and a doctor. It still had about 300 people in 1915.

vs-2336663.st: Dodge (1973): Clowry was on the Chicago & North Western between Michigamme and Ishpeming, a few miles northeast of Champion, on part of the Clowry homestead. Its post office ran only from 22 May 1892 to 4 May 1894; it was still listed as a station in 1910 and 1927.

m-rep-michigamme-1906.st: Dodge (1973): Michigamme grew on an iron find of 1872; the Michigamme Mine produced nearly a million tons of ore in its 33 years before closing in 1905. vs-2336634.st: Dodge (1973): Sands was a station on the Chicago & North Western 9 miles from Marquette in Chocolay Township, settled in 1874 and named for the lumberman Louie Sands; the village stood a mile back from the station. Its post office opened on 23 January 1878, and in 1887 it had about 200 people, with charcoal burning, a wagon maker and a general store.

vs-2336629.st: Dodge (1973): Swanzy was the post-office name for Chesire Junction, about 5 miles from Forsyth on the Chicago & North Western in Forsyth Township. Its post office ran from October 1889 to 1905, when it had about 200 people, iron mines of the Escanaba River Land & Iron Company, a lumber dealer and a general store.

pmi98-carbondale-station.st: Dodge (1973): In 1887 Carbondale was a recently settled stop of about 50 people on the Chicago & North Western, 12 miles north of Menominee, with James W. Osborne's post office, general store and cedar business. Its post office ran from December 1881 to April 1904.

pme12-hathorn-1912.st: Dodge (1973): Faithorn (the 1912 plat's "Hathorn") was first called Pembina and was renamed for N. vs-2353171.st: Dodge (1973): Faunus was a Chicago & North Western stop, one of several the railroad named from ancient mythology. Its post office ran from 1896 to 1908, and nothing remained by 1973.

pme12-guerley.st: Dodge (1973): Gourley (the 1912 plat's "Guerley") had about 100 people in 1905, in Cedarville Township, with the Mashek Lumber Company's mill. vs-2353168.st: Dodge (1973): Ingallston was first called Section 19; the Ingalls brothers of Menominee set up a sawmill here in 1866. pmi98-talbot-station.st: Dodge (1973): Talbot, also called Gravel Pit, was named for Samuel H. Talbot of a lumbering firm; in 1887 it had about 60 people in Nadeau Township, settled in 1879, with Fred W. Sensiba's post office and store and several logging jobbers.

m-ghost-calderwood.st: Dodge (1973): Calderwood was named for the Calderwood Lumber Company, a logging and sawmill outfit organized by Minnesota men; it was settled in 1900 and had a new post office in 1909. By 1915 it had about 100 people in Interior Township, 9 miles from Trout Creek, and in 1927 a Congregational church and telephone service.

wd2-43.st: Dodge (1973): Matchwood was the 1888 headquarters of the Diamond Match Company, set up to supply its many logging camps, hence the name; its post office opened on 23 April 1889, and in 1893 it had about 100 people on the Duluth, South Shore & Atlantic, with a hotel and stores.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

vs-2125251.st: Dodge (1973): Paulding was a post office and Chicago & North Western station about 5 miles south of Trout Creek, with a post office from about 1893 to 1904. It reopened on 1 May 1936 and had 29 people in 1938.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

vs-2125243.st: Dodge (1973): Rousseau began as Hubbell's Mills, a new post office called Rubicon in 1893, and was renamed in 1920 for Edward Rousseau, supervisor of Bohemian Township for 27 years. It had about 325 people in 1927, with loggers and a general store, and was still on the 1970 highway map.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

vs-2125238.st: Dodge (1973): Wainola was settled by Finns in 1887 and named for a legendary Finnish name. It had about 300 people in 1915 and 425 in 1927, in Greenland Township near Mass, with Finnish Evangelical and Lutheran churches, a sawmill, loggers and general stores; the post office closed on 31 October 1939.
src: Dodge, Michigan Ghost Towns of the Upper Peninsula (1973; Glendon 1990 reprint), your screenshots

m-ghost-kearsarge.st: Dodge (1973): Phillipsville, listed under Kearsarge in the 1927 directory, is one of the old mine locations strung along US-41 between Mohawk and Calumet; in 1973 a two-story insulbrick building with an antique shop and a "Phillipsville" sign marked it.
